title: Where caches live and how they fill
summary: The cache layers between a user and the database, cache-aside versus read-through, write-through, write-behind and write-around, and why you delete on write instead of updating.

steps.title: A cache at every hop
body: A **cache** is a copy of data kept closer to the reader than the source of truth. Every hop on the way to
the database can hold one:
```text
browser ──> CDN edge ──> reverse proxy ──> app server ──> distributed cache ──> database
(HTTP       (seconds    (nginx/Envoy      (in-process      (Redis / Valkey     (source of
cache)      to days)    micro-cache)      memory, ns)      cluster, ~0.5 ms)   truth, ms)
| Layer | Typical hit cost | Shared by | Invalidate with |
| Browser | 0 (no request) | one user | `Cache-Control`, versioned URLs |
| CDN edge | 5-30 ms from the user | a region of users | TTL, purge API |
| In-process (near cache) | ~100 ns | one app instance | short TTL, a pub/sub message |
| Distributed cache | ~0.2-1 ms in the same AZ | every app instance | delete the key |
The closer the cache, the cheaper the hit, and the **harder it is to invalidate**: you can delete one
Redis key in a millisecond, but you cannot reach into 40,000 browsers. That trade-off decides what each
layer may hold.

steps.prompt: Where would you cache each of these? Pick the layer closest to the user that is still safe.
items: The product page HTML for logged-out visitors
The feature-flag set, re-read every 30 s
A user's shopping cart, read on every page
Rendered product details shared by all app servers
The current balance shown before a payment is approved
explain: A hashed bundle never changes, so the browser can keep it for a year. Feature flags are tiny and read
constantly: an in-process copy with a short refresh is ideal. A cart must look the same on every server,
so it belongs in a shared cache (or the database). A balance used to approve a payment must come from the
source of truth: a stale read there costs real money.

steps.title: Five ways to fill and write
body: - **Cache-aside** (lazy loading): the app reads the cache; on a miss it reads the database and puts the
value in the cache. On a write it updates the database and **deletes** the cache key. The most common
pattern, because the cache can fail and the app still works (slowly).
- **Read-through**: the cache library itself loads misses from the database (a loader function). Same
shape as cache-aside, but the loading code lives in one place.
- **Write-through**: every write goes to the cache and the database together, so the cache is always warm
for recent writes. Costs a cache write per database write, even for data nobody reads.
- **Write-behind** (write-back): the write lands in the cache and is flushed to the database later in
batches. Fast writes, but a cache crash **loses data** that was acknowledged. Rarely the right call for
business data.
- **Write-around**: writes go only to the database; the cache fills on the next read. Good for data that
is written often and read rarely (logs, bulk imports).
```text
cache-aside read:   GET key ──hit──> return
└─miss──> SELECT ... ──> SET key value EX 300 ──> return
cache-aside write:  UPDATE ... ──> DEL key

steps.prompt: Match each pattern to its defining behaviour.
pairs: The app loads misses itself and deletes the key after a write
The cache calls a loader function on a miss
Each write updates the cache and the database together
Writes are acknowledged from the cache and flushed to the database later
Writes skip the cache; the next read fills it
steps.explain: In an interview, name the pattern and its failure mode: write-behind loses acknowledged writes when the cache dies; write-through pays for writes nobody reads; cache-aside serves a miss storm when the cache is empty.

steps.prompt: Put a cache-aside **read** of product 42 in order.
lines: On a miss, SELECT the row from the database
Return the value to the caller
steps.explain: Setting a TTL on fill is the safety net: even if an invalidation is lost, a stale value lives at most one TTL.

steps.title: Delete on write, and the race that remains
body: Why **delete** the key instead of writing the new value into the cache? Two writers can interleave:
```text
t1  writer A: UPDATE price = 10            t3  writer B: SET cache = 12
t2  writer B: UPDATE price = 12            t4  writer A: SET cache = 10   <- cache says 10, DB says 12, forever
With delete-on-write, both writers just `DEL`, and the next reader loads the true value. One race is
left: a **slow reader** reads the old row, a writer updates and deletes, then the slow reader puts the
old row back into the cache. It is rare (the read must be slower than a whole write), and three things
bound it:
1. A **TTL** on every key: the stale value dies within one TTL.
2. A **version** (or `updated_at`) stored with the value: only `SET` if the version is newer (a Lua
script or `SET ... NX` on a versioned key).
3. A **delayed second delete** a few hundred milliseconds after the write, for hot keys.
Rule of thumb: decide how stale each piece of data may be ("prices: 1 minute, stock count: never shown
from cache at checkout"), and pick the TTL from that, not from a habit.

prompt: **Symptom first.** After a price change, some customers see the old price for exactly 24 hours, then it
fixes itself. The code updates the database and then runs this:
code: await db.ExecuteAsync("UPDATE products SET price = @p WHERE id = @id", new { p, id });
options: Two concurrent writes can leave the older value in the cache, and the 24 h TTL keeps it there; delete the key instead and use a TTL that matches how stale a price may be
Redis lost the write; switch to write-behind
The database is lagging; read prices from the primary
The TTL is too short; raise it to 7 days
steps.explain: Writing the value into the cache after the update is exactly the interleaving race. Exactly 24 hours of staleness is the fingerprint of the TTL bounding the damage. `KeyDeleteAsync` plus a shorter TTL fixes both halves.

steps.title: A cache-aside wrapper
prompt: Write a class `CacheAside` over a database (a `Dictionary<string, string>`) with its own in-memory cache:
- `string? Get(string key)`: return the cached value on a hit. On a miss, read the database (count it in
`DbReads`), cache the value and return it. A key missing from the database returns `null` and is **not**
- `void Update(string key, string value)`: write the database, then **delete** the cached copy.
Reading `p1` twice costs one database read; after `Update("p1", ...)` the next read goes to the database
starter: public void Update(string key, string value) { }
solution: public CacheAside(Dictionary<string, string> db) { this.db = db; }
public int DbReads { get; private set; }
if (cache.TryGetValue(key, out var hit)) return hit;
if (!db.TryGetValue(key, out var row)) return null;
public void Update(string key, string value)
hints: Keep a second dictionary for the cache. `Get` tries it first with `TryGetValue`.
`Update` writes `db[key] = value;` and then `cache.Remove(key);`: never `cache[key] = value`.
template: Dojo.Eq("first read of p1 comes from the database", "9.99", dojoC.Get("p1"));
Dojo.Eq("second read of p1 is a hit", "9.99", dojoC.Get("p1"));
Dojo.Eq("one database read so far", 1, dojoC.DbReads);
Dojo.Eq("the database has the new price", "8.99", dojoDb["p1"]);
Dojo.Check("Update deletes the cached copy", !dojoC.IsCached("p1"), "after Update, p1 should not be in the cache");
Dojo.Eq("the next read sees the new price", "8.99", dojoC.Get("p1"));
Dojo.Eq("that read went to the database", 2, dojoC.DbReads);
Dojo.Eq("a key missing from the database returns null", (string?)null, dojoC.Get("nope"));
Dojo.Check("missing keys are not cached", !dojoC.IsCached("nope"), "nope should not be cached");
Dojo.Eq("each read of a missing key costs a database read", 4, dojoC.DbReads);
explain: Not caching misses is a choice. Under attack (requests for random ids that do not exist) every request
reaches the database; the usual fix is **negative caching**: store a short-lived "not found" marker.

steps.title: Build it: cache the catalogue
prompt: In the **System design board**, open *Cache the catalogue*. A read-heavy catalogue with skewed keys is
overloading its database. Add a cache cluster in front of the database (cache-aside from the app servers),
size it for the hot set rather than the whole catalogue, and run the load test until the database
utilisation and p99 goals are met within the budget.
steps.explain: Watch the cache hit rate panel: a cache that holds a few percent of the keys can still serve most reads when the traffic is skewed. That is the next lesson.
